questions.q: What is red-teaming, as described in this lesson?
options: Adversarial testing of an already-trained model, deliberately trying to elicit harmful or unwanted behavior before deployment
A training-time technique that replaces RLHF
A method for labeling preference data more cheaply
A way to automatically fix a model's weights without retraining
questions.explain: Red-teaming happens after training, on a model that already exists, with testers deliberately trying to make it fail in order to find problems before real users do.

questions.q: Why does red-teaming matter even after a model has gone through RLHF, RLAIF, or Constitutional AI?
options: Because those training methods have no effect on model behavior at all
Because it replaces the need for any reward model
Because red-teaming is required by law in every jurisdiction
Because red-teaming assumes that training-time alignment work was imperfect and looks for the specific gaps it left
questions.explain: Red-teaming is a deployment-time check built on the assumption — well supported by the limits covered in this chapter — that training-time methods don't fully close every gap.

questions.q: What is a key strength of automated red-teaming compared to manual red-teaming?
options: It is better at inventing entirely novel attack strategies nobody has thought of
It can generate and test a much larger volume of adversarial prompts, covering breadth and variations quickly
It requires no model to generate test prompts
It eliminates the need for any human review of results
questions.explain: A model can generate and test far more adversarial prompts than a human team, which makes automated red-teaming strong on scale and coverage of known attack patterns, though weaker at genuinely novel ideas.

questions.q: Why do labs bring in external, third-party red-teamers rather than relying only on their internal teams?
options: Internal teams are legally prohibited from red-teaming their own models
External testers are always better at every category of attack than internal staff
External testers bring different backgrounds and assumptions, helping surface blind spots the internal team's shared assumptions might miss
Internal red-teaming is technically impossible to set up
questions.explain: An internal team shares the lab's own assumptions about how the system is 'supposed' to be used. Outside testers, from different backgrounds and use cases, probe from different angles.

questions.q: How does red-teaming fit together with the training-time methods covered earlier in this chapter?
options: It finds where training-time methods fell short, and those findings feed back into further training or policy changes
It replaces RLHF and Constitutional AI entirely
It has no relationship to training-time alignment methods
It is only used before any training-time method is applied
questions.explain: Red-teaming doesn't train a model itself — it surfaces failure modes that training didn't catch, which then inform further rounds of training or policy adjustments.
